client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother died six months ago. Every time I go out with friends or try to be social, I just feel this hollow emptiness, like I'm watching everyone else laugh and have fun from behind a glass wall. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something because I can't keep living like this.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out, especially when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I want you to know that feeling of being separated from the world, like you're watching life happen through glass, makes complete sense given the profound loss you've been carrying. Grief has a way of quietly disconnecting us from the things that used to feel natural and joyful. I'm wondering — when you're in those moments with friends and that emptiness settles in, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind?

client: Honestly, the main thing that runs through my head is something like, "How can they just laugh like nothing happened?" And then right after that comes this guilt, like I'm somehow betraying my brother by even being there, trying to have a good time when he's just... gone. It's like I don't feel like I deserve to enjoy anything right now, and that thought kind of poisons the whole night before it even really starts.
therapist: That thought — that you don't deserve to enjoy anything — is such a heavy burden to carry into every social situation, and it makes so much sense that it would drain the night before it even begins. In CBT, we'd call this a kind of "grief rule" you've unconsciously set for yourself, where enjoyment feels like a betrayal rather than something your brother might have actually wanted for you. I'm curious — if the situation were reversed, and it was your brother who was still here grieving you, what would you have wanted *him* to allow himself to feel?

client: I mean... obviously I would have wanted him to still live his life, to laugh sometimes, to not just shut down completely. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling it in my gut are two completely different things, and right now my gut just wins every time. It's like I can see the logic of what you're saying, but it doesn't actually touch the feeling when I'm standing there in the middle of a group of people and the emptiness just hits.
therapist: What you're describing — that gap between knowing something and *feeling* it — is one of the most honest and important things you can recognize in grief work, and it tells me you're not broken or stuck, you're just at the beginning of a process that takes time to move from the head down into the heart. The logic is already there, which is actually meaningful, but you're right that thoughts alone don't automatically rewire what the body has learned to feel in those moments. I'm wondering — when that emptiness hits in a crowd, where do you actually feel it physically, and has there ever been even one small moment, however brief, where the wall felt slightly thinner?

client: Physically it's like this heaviness right in the center of my chest, and sometimes my throat gets tight like I'm about to cry even when no tears actually come. As for a moment where the wall felt thinner... there was this one time a few weeks ago when my friend told a story about something stupid and embarrassing that happened to her, and I actually laughed, like a real laugh, and for maybe two seconds I wasn't thinking about any of it. But then I immediately felt awful about it, like I'd just proved I didn't care enough about my brother, so I don't know if that even counts as a good thing.
therapist: That moment absolutely counts — in fact, it's one of the most important things you've shared, because your body and heart *remembered* how to be alive for two seconds, and that wasn't a betrayal, that was proof that your brother's loss hasn't destroyed you completely. The guilt that rushed in right after is so understandable, but I want to gently offer this: that laugh didn't mean you don't care enough — it might actually be the part of you that's still fighting to survive this. What do you think your brother would have said if he'd seen you genuinely laugh at your friend's story?

client: He would have laughed too, honestly, he had this whole thing where he loved seeing me caught off guard and actually losing it over something dumb. But even saying that out loud right now, I notice I'm already trying to talk myself out of it, like maybe I'm just telling myself that because it's the easier thing to believe. I don't know how to trust that thought when the guilt feels so much more real and solid than anything else right now.
therapist: The fact that you can picture him laughing with you so specifically — that's not wishful thinking, that's you actually *knowing* your brother. And I want to gently point out something important: you just caught yourself in the act of dismissing a true and loving thought, which takes real self-awareness, and that instinct to talk yourself out of comfort is worth paying attention to. Guilt often feels more "trustworthy" than warmth in grief because it mistakes intensity for truth — but feeling something strongly doesn't automatically make it accurate. What do you notice happens in your body when you let yourself sit with the image of him laughing alongside you, even just for a moment?

client: When I actually let myself picture it, that heaviness in my chest shifts a little, like it loosens just slightly, and for a second it almost feels warm instead of just empty. But then I get scared of that warmth, like if I lean into it too much I'm going to lose the grief somehow, and losing the grief feels like losing him all over again. I know that probably sounds strange, but the pain is the last thing I have that still feels connected to him.
therapist: That doesn't sound strange at all — it sounds like one of the most profound and tender things a grieving person can discover about themselves, and it shows how deeply you loved him. But I want to offer you a gentle reframe: what if the warmth you felt in that image *is* the connection to him, just as real as the pain, and grief doesn't have to mean holding onto suffering to prove love? The heaviness loosening when you pictured him laughing — that wasn't you losing him, that was him, in some way, still reaching you. What if love, not just pain, could be the thing that keeps you connected to who he was?

client: That idea is... I want to believe it, and part of me does, but I'm also scared that if I start letting the warmth replace the pain, I'll slowly stop thinking about him as much, like the grief is the thing that keeps him present in my daily life. It's hard to explain, but the pain feels like a ritual almost, like it's the price I pay to keep him close. I guess I'm not sure I'm ready to give that up yet, even if holding onto it is making me miserable.
therapist: What you just described — grief as a ritual, as the price of keeping him present — is one of the most deeply human things I've heard, and you don't have to give that up, not today, not on anyone else's timeline. But I want to sit with something you said: you're not being asked to choose between pain and him, because *he* isn't the pain — he's the laugh that caught you off guard, the warmth in your chest just now, the person who loved seeing you lose it over something dumb. What if the ritual slowly shifted, not disappearing, but expanding to include those living memories of him alongside the grief?

client: That distinction you're making, between him and the pain, I've never actually thought about it that way before, and something about it lands differently than I expected. Like maybe I've been so focused on holding the grief tight that I've actually been keeping a smaller version of him, just the loss of him, instead of the whole person he was. I'm not sure I know how to do what you're describing in practice, but for the first time tonight I don't feel completely resistant to trying.
therapist: What you just recognized — that you've been holding a smaller version of him — is genuinely profound, and the fact that something has shifted enough that you're open to trying tells me this work has already begun. In practice, it can start very small, like when that guilt rushes in after a real laugh, gently asking yourself "what else was he, beyond this loss?" and letting one true memory of him as a whole person answer back. You don't have to overhaul anything overnight — what would feel like one tiny, manageable way you could invite the fuller version of him into your week?

client: There's this old playlist he made for me a couple years ago that I haven't been able to open since he died, and maybe I could try listening to just one song from it this week, not forcing myself through the whole thing. But I'm already worried that it'll just wreck me and I'll spend the rest of the day unable to function, which is part of why I've been avoiding it. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to do something like that without it just becoming another reason to fall apart.
therapist: That idea — one song, not the whole playlist — shows real wisdom about your own limits, and it's a beautiful way to meet him again on your own terms. One thing that can help is to plan a small "landing" for yourself beforehand: choose a specific, gentle thing you'll do right after, like making a cup of tea or texting a friend, so that if the feelings do come, you're not just left alone in the aftermath but held by something small and grounding. What would feel like a safe enough moment this week — maybe a time when you have a little space around you — where you could try that one song without it needing to go perfectly?

client: Sunday mornings are usually quiet for me, I don't have anywhere to be and my roommate is typically out, so that's probably the most realistic time. I like the idea of having something planned after, though I'd probably pick making coffee rather than texting someone, because I'm not sure I'd want to have to explain to a friend why I'm suddenly emotional out of nowhere. The part that still worries me is what if one song turns into me sitting there for an hour just spiraling, because I don't have the best track record of knowing when to stop when the grief gets going.
therapist: Sunday morning with your coffee sounds like a genuinely thoughtful and caring container for this — and choosing coffee over explaining yourself to someone is you already knowing what you need, which matters. For the spiraling worry, we can build in a simple "exit ramp" beforehand: decide in advance that when the song ends, you get up physically, move to the kitchen, and start the coffee — the body moving can interrupt the mind's pull to stay under the wave. What if the rule for this week was simply "one song and then I stand up," giving yourself full permission to feel whatever comes, but also full permission to stop there?
